one_liner: C-ABI (LD_PRELOAD-able) build of the Rust memx crate; memmem 2.7-5.9x faster than glibc/musl, other mem* mixed.
what_it_does: A small Rust crate built as a cdylib, staticlib and rlib that exports memchr, memrchr, memcmp, bcmp, memmem and memset (and memcpy only when the default no_memcpy feature is off and the target is not musl) under their libc names, each a thin wrapper that turns the C pointers into slices and calls the memx crate. It is meant to be injected into an existing Linux binary with LD_PRELOAD or linked ahead of libc. There is no prefixed C API (a header can be generated with cbindgen via the Makefile), so you replace the libc symbols wholesale rather than calling it per call site.
how_it_is_fast: memx picks SSE2 or AVX2 kernels at run time (cpufeatures, cached in a static AtomicPtr after the first call), with unrolled 16/32-byte compare loops, alignment prologues and software prefetch; non-x86 targets use generic SWAR code. memmem is a 'stochastic naive' search (the author's naive_opt idea): it looks up the first and last needle bytes in a hard-coded English/source-code frequency table, runs a SIMD memchr for the rarer one and does a full SIMD compare at each candidate. On text with a rare boundary byte this is mostly one vectorised memchr pass, avoiding the per-call setup of glibc's and musl's two-way/hashed memmem.
when_to_use: x86-64 Linux C or C++ programs whose hot path is memmem over text (log scanning, grep-like filters, protocol parsing of ASCII) where you can test LD_PRELOAD or relink
musl-linked x86-64 binaries (e.g. Alpine containers): the tables show memchr about 2.0x, memcmp up to 3.8x and memmem 5.0-5.9x faster than musl's simple C routines
Quick experiments to see whether mem* routines matter for an existing binary without recompiling it
Rust code wanting the same routines: use the memx crate directly (it is what was benchmarked) rather than the C exports
when_not_to_use: Blanket LD_PRELOAD on glibc systems: in the same tables memx's memcmp is 0.56x of glibc (en), bcmp about 0.8x and memset 0.59x on the short case, and memchr is within 10%; only memmem is a clear win, and there is no switch to export memmem alone

memmem over untrusted or repetitive input: the naive candidate-and-verify search is O(haystack x needle) in the worst case, whereas glibc and musl use linear-time two-way search; the frequency weights are tuned for English text and source code, not binary data
Non-x86 targets: SIMD paths exist only for x86 and x86-64 (aarch64 only gained a prefetch helper); other architectures run the generic SWAR fallback
Statically linked musl builds that need memcpy (duplicate memcpy symbol, noted in src/lib.rs), or code that needs memmove, strlen, strchr and other string.h functions, which are not provided
Environments without a Rust toolchain: there are no prebuilt binaries beyond what cargo deb produces locally

integration.dependencies: Rust toolchain to build; crates libc 0.2 and memx 0.2 (memx pulls cpufeatures 0.2 on x86, x86-64 and aarch64). Also usable as a staticlib or as a Rust crate (call memx_cdy::memx_init() to force linking).
integration.platforms: x86 and x86-64 for the SSE2/AVX2 paths (run-time dispatch); other targets use generic code; the LD_PRELOAD workflow is Linux/ELF-specific (CI builds on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows)
integration.thread_safety: Stateless functions; the dispatch pointer is a static AtomicPtr set on first call with a benign race, so concurrent calls are safe; not otherwise documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same C signatures and symbol names, so LD_PRELOAD replaces libc's memchr, memrchr, memcmp, bcmp, memmem and memset as a set; memcpy is not exported in the default build, and calls inside glibc itself or compiler-inlined constant-size mem* calls are not affected

gotchas: Benchmark scope: the memx docs tables (rustc 1.69.0, i5-4570, 2023) time memx's Rust functions, not memx-cdy's C exports or the LD_PRELOAD path, and predate memx 0.2.1 (2026-05-23), which rewrote every core and x86 loop; the en memmem needle 'just before we went into the very simple problem' starts with 'j', which has weight 0 (rarest) in memx's _ASCII_STOCHAS table and occurs only twice in the 16 KB of test lines, so that row measures little more than one AVX2 memchr pass, the best case for this algorithm.

Unsound boundary: the exports are safe extern "C" fns that call slice::from_raw_parts on caller pointers, so memchr(NULL, c, 0) or memcmp(NULL, NULL, 0), which C programs pass and glibc tolerates (and C23 defines for n = 0), is undefined behaviour in Rust, and Rust code can trigger it without unsafe; issue #2 ('Unsound usages of unsafe implementation about c_void', 2026-06-08) is open with no reply.

Self-interposition risk: the crate exports libc names without #![no_builtins], and 0.1.13 (2023-10-09) had to fix a stack overflow on a 3-byte memcmp by bypassing memx for n < 4, consistent with the exported memcmp ending up calling itself; any path that the compiler lowers back to memset/memcmp/bcmp inside the preloaded library can recurse the same way.

memcmp and bcmp return only -1, 0 or 1 (valid C, but different from glibc's byte difference), and memx's memcpy, which is 3.1x faster than musl in the tables, can never be reached on musl through memx-cdy because the export is compiled out there.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over AOCL-LibMem when you want a portable x86-64 memmem/memchr injection on any vendor's CPU and especially on musl (AOCL-LibMem targets glibc on AMD Zen and publishes no numbers), and over sliceslice when the caller is C or C++ and cannot build a reusable searcher object; for memcpy or memset wins on glibc pick something else, since memx loses there.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel i5-4570 with rustc 1.69.0 (opt-level 3, LTO, one codegen unit), Criterion time per pass over 21 text lines (about 16 KB English or 32 KB Japanese) shows memx's memmem at 0.80 us versus glibc's 2.17 us (2.7x) and musl's 3.95 us (5.0x) on English, and 3.1x and 5.9x on Japanese; memchr is 1.07-1.09x faster than glibc and about 2x faster than musl, while memcmp, bcmp, memset and memcpy are slower than glibc on the short English case. These are memx crate numbers with glibc and musl called through Rust FFI; libc versions are not stated.
status_note: The wrapper changes rarely (0.2.0 on 2025-09-24, last commit 2026-06-03 a changelog reformat; 4 stars, about 41k crates.io downloads) while memx itself is active (0.2.2 on 2026-05-27, about 472k downloads); MIT OR Apache-2.0, so it is easy to adopt, but the published benchmark tables have not been regenerated since memx's 2026 rewrite.
